script.opening: "For a while now, whenever I use condoms or wear rubber washing-up gloves, I get itchy, red and a bit swollen where they touch. Once my lips tingled too. Could I be allergic to latex? And what do I do about contraception?"

facts.text: About 6 months. Within minutes of contact with latex condoms or washing-up gloves: itchy, raised, red and swollen skin where they touch. Settles within an hour or two after removal. Once, blowing up balloons for her niece’s party, her lips tingled and felt a bit puffy — settled by itself.
Never throat tightness, wheeze, breathlessness, faintness or widespread hives. Never needed hospital or adrenaline.
Mouth goes itchy with kiwi fruit; hasn’t eaten avocado much. Bananas fine. No other food allergies known.
Hay fever and mild eczema as a child. Works as a dental nurse — the practice uses nitrile gloves, so no problem at work. Never had operations. No spina bifida.

Uses condoms with her partner of a year; nothing else. Not keen on hormones — "the pill made me moody years ago". Not pregnant; last period 10 days ago. Due a cervical screening test next month (only if asked).
No regular medicines. No known drug allergies. Non-smoker.

Practical, a bit anxious about the lip tingling. Ask "Could it become dangerous?" and "Do I need one of those adrenaline pens?" Interested in latex-free condoms, but wants time to think about other contraception.

ice.ideas: "I read about latex allergy online — I think that’s what it is."
ice.concerns: "The lip thing scared me. Could it get worse?" And "I don’t want to get pregnant."
ice.expectations: "To know for sure, and to sort out contraception."

cues: "Once my lips tingled" — assess anaphylaxis risk.
"My mouth itches with kiwi" (if foods are asked) — latex-fruit cross-reactivity.
"What do I do about contraception?" — latex-free options and choices.

checkpoints.text: Recognises LATEX ALLERGY — immediate (IgE/type I) reactions (itching, urticaria, angioedema, potential anaphylaxis) on latex contact — and distinguishes delayed (type IV) contact dermatitis

Takes a history (including systemic features around the lip episode) and identifies RISK GROUPS (healthcare workers, spina bifida/multiple surgeries, atopy) and occupational exposure (asks about her job and gloves at work)
Asks about/advises on LATEX-FRUIT cross-reactivity (banana, avocado, kiwi, chestnut)

Arranges confirmation/REFERRAL to allergy/immunology where indicated (specific IgE/skin testing) and ASSESSES ANAPHYLAXIS risk — providing an emergency plan, with an adrenaline auto-injector (two devices, MHRA June 2023) considered with the allergy service if systemic-reaction risk (NICE NG258)

Advises strict AVOIDANCE with latex-free alternatives (polyurethane/polyisoprene condoms, nitrile gloves), informing healthcare/dentists/cervical screening sample-taker/employers (COSHH), MedicAlert, and sorts NON-LATEX contraception with slippage and emergency contraception advice; documents the allergy
Explains the diagnosis and plan, addresses the contraception concern directly, and checks understanding
Checks her understanding of the diagnosis and the importance of avoidance, and agrees a practical plan for alternatives at home, at work and in healthcare settings that fits her life

Safety-nets and follows up: anaphylaxis-risk plan/auto-injector if relevant, allergy referral, avoidance and alternatives, informing providers before procedures, and review — recognition + avoidance + safety planning

worked.txt: "Yes — immediate itching, redness and swelling whenever latex touches your skin, with your lips tingling once, strongly suggests a latex allergy. That’s different from a slow rash to rubber chemicals; yours is the immediate type."

"What’s your job — do you work with gloves, like in healthcare, cleaning or catering? If so, your employer has to reduce your exposure, usually by switching to non-latex gloves. And do you react to certain fruits — banana, avocado, kiwi or chestnut? They cross-react with latex, so it’s worth knowing."

"The most important thing is safety. Because latex allergy can occasionally cause a severe whole-body reaction, I want to know if you’ve ever had breathing or throat symptoms. If there’s any risk, we’d make an emergency plan, and the allergy specialist would decide about adrenaline pens — if prescribed, you’d carry two at all times — and you must tell any dentist, hospital or nurse, including for cervical screening, before procedures so they use latex-free."
"The key is avoiding latex — use nitrile gloves instead of rubber ones, avoid balloons, and for condoms there are excellent latex-free ones made of polyurethane or polyisoprene."

"For contraception, you can use non-latex condoms — they can slip or break a little more often, so use plenty of lubricant and know how to get emergency contraception — or we could consider a method that doesn’t involve latex at all — the pill, an implant or coil — if you’d prefer not to rely on condoms. Condoms still protect against infections."

"I’ll refer you to the allergy clinic to confirm it with testing, record the allergy clearly in your notes, and suggest a medical-alert bracelet. If you ever get swelling of your tongue or throat, difficulty breathing, a hoarse voice or feel faint after latex, call 999 straight away — that’s urgent."

f.learning: LATEX ALLERGY causes immediate (IgE-mediated, type I) reactions on latex contact — itching, redness, urticaria, angioedema (swelling) and potentially ANAPHYLAXIS — from condoms, rubber gloves, balloons and similar, and must be distinguished from a delayed (type IV) contact dermatitis to rubber-accelerator chemicals (eczematous, 24–48h). Take a history (which products, immediacy/severity, systemic features, occupational exposure — ask her job — atopy) and recognise RISK GROUPS: healthcare workers, people with spina bifida or multiple surgeries (repeated latex exposure), and atopic individuals. Ask about and advise on the LATEX-FRUIT cross-reactivity syndrome — banana, avocado, kiwi, chestnut and others — which can cause allergic reactions. Arrange confirmation/referral to allergy/immunology where indicated (specific IgE/skin-prick testing), and critically ASSESS ANAPHYLAXIS risk: where there is a history of or risk of systemic reactions, provide an emergency action plan, with an adrenaline auto-injector decided with the allergy service (two in-date devices if prescribed, MHRA Drug Safety Update June 2023; specialist allergy referral after any anaphylaxis, NICE NG258 2026), and ensure the patient informs healthcare providers/dentists before procedures so a latex-free environment is used. Manage with strict AVOIDANCE and latex-free alternatives (polyurethane/polyisoprene condoms, nitrile gloves), advise informing employers (who must control exposure under COSHH 2002), dentists and healthcare providers and a MedicAlert, and for CONTRACEPTION offer non-latex condoms (explaining slightly higher slippage/breakage and emergency contraception) or an alternative method so the patient is not reliant on latex (FSRH) — documenting the allergy clearly (NICE CG183) and telling the cervical screening sample-taker. The skill is recognising latex allergy, avoidance/cross-reactivity advice, anaphylaxis-risk assessment/planning, allergy referral and practical alternatives.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG258 (2026) Anaphylaxis: assessment and referral after emergency treatment · [2] Resuscitation Council UK, Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021) · [3] MHRA Drug Safety Update (June 2023), adrenaline auto-injectors: new guidance and resources for safe use · [4] NICE CG183 (2014) Drug allergy: diagnosis and management, recording allergy status · [5] FSRH Clinical Guideline: Barrier methods for contraception and STI prevention (2012) · [6] Health and Safety Executive guidance on latex and the Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002
knowledge.summary: Itching, redness and swelling within minutes of latex contact, with lip tingling, suggests immediate (IgE-mediated) latex allergy. Assess for any systemic features, refer to an allergy service to confirm it, and advise strict avoidance with latex-free condoms and nitrile gloves. Record the allergy, warn her to tell every healthcare and dental team, ask about cross-reacting fruits, and give clear emergency advice. Sort out contraception so she is not relying on latex.

points.t: Immediate (type I, IgE) latex allergy causes itch, hives and swelling within minutes of contact and can progress to anaphylaxis, especially with mucosal exposure. Delayed (type IV) allergic contact dermatitis to rubber accelerator chemicals gives an eczematous rash 1–2 days later. Irritant dermatitis from gloves is commoner still. Her quick reactions and lip tingling fit type I.
Healthcare, cleaning and catering workers who wear gloves; people with spina bifida or many operations; and people with atopy [6]. Ask about her work and any occupational exposure.
Some people with latex allergy react to foods such as banana, avocado, kiwi and chestnut. Ask about reactions to these and advise caution.

Refer to an allergy service for specific IgE or skin-prick testing and advice. Ask about throat tightness, wheeze, faintness or widespread hives: any systemic reaction raises the stakes. Adrenaline auto-injectors are for people at risk of anaphylaxis; if prescribed, she should carry two in-date devices and know how to use them [3]. Anyone treated for anaphylaxis should be referred to a specialist allergy service [1][2].

Use non-latex condoms (polyurethane or polyisoprene) [5] and nitrile gloves; avoid balloons. Tell dentists, hospitals and every healthcare team before any procedure, so they use latex-free equipment. Record the allergy clearly in her notes [4]; a medical alert bracelet can help in an emergency.

Offer non-latex condoms and discuss other methods that do not rely on latex, such as the pill, implant, injection or intrauterine methods, with condoms still advised for STI protection [5]. Some non-latex condoms may break or slip slightly more often, so explain correct use and emergency contraception [5].
If she wears latex gloves at work, her employer must assess and control exposure under COSHH, usually by switching to non-latex gloves [6]. An occupational health referral may help.

Occupation and glove use; impact on sex life and contraception; worry after the lip episode.
Referral for specific IgE or skin-prick testing; no in-practice challenge; records allergy status.

Probable immediate (IgE-mediated) latex allergy with local reactions only.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

model.text: Hello, Ms Boyd, I’m Dr Shah. How can I help today?

For a while now, whenever I use condoms or wear rubber washing-up gloves, I get itchy, red and a bit swollen where they touch. Once my lips tingled too. Could I be allergic to latex? And what do I do about contraception?
Thank you for coming in about this; it sounds uncomfortable and worrying. I’ll ask some questions about the reactions first, then we’ll sort out both the allergy and your contraception.
model.why: Acknowledges both agendas and sets the plan

model.text: Great, thanks.
When you touch latex, how quickly does the reaction start, and how long does it last?
model.why: Timing distinguishes type I from type IV

model.text: Within minutes. It calms down after an hour or two once I take them off.
Is it raised, itchy lumps like nettle rash, or a dry, scaly rash that appears the next day?
Itchy, raised and swollen, straight away.
When your lips tingled, did you have any swelling of your tongue or throat, difficulty breathing, wheezing, a hoarse voice, feeling faint, or a rash all over?
No. Just the tingling, and it settled by itself.
Where do you come across latex most? Do you wear gloves at work at all?
Just the washing-up gloves at home, as far as I know.
Have you had operations, or do you have asthma, eczema or hay fever?
Nothing I can think of.
Have you ever reacted to foods like banana, avocado, kiwi or chestnuts? Some people with latex allergy do.
Not that I’ve noticed.
And for contraception, what are you using at the moment, apart from condoms?
Just condoms. That’s why I’m stuck.
What have you been thinking this might be, and what worries you most?
I read about latex allergy online. The lip thing scared me. Could it get worse? And I don’t want to get pregnant.
Both of those are really sensible worries, and we’ll deal with each one.
I think you’re right: this sounds like an immediate latex allergy. The fast, itchy swelling where latex touches is typical. It’s different from a slow skin rash to rubber chemicals.
model.why: Names type I latex allergy and the difference from type IV

model.text: Could it become dangerous?

Most reactions stay local, like yours, but latex allergy can occasionally cause a severe whole-body reaction, especially when latex touches the lips, mouth or genitals. So I’d like an allergy specialist to confirm it with a test and advise on your risk.
Do I need one of those adrenaline pens?

You haven’t had any breathing, throat or faint symptoms, so I won’t give one today, but the specialist will decide. If they prescribe one, you’d carry two at all times. And you’ll know exactly what to do in an emergency before you leave.
model.why: Anaphylaxis risk assessment; AAI decision explained

model.text: The key is avoiding latex. Use nitrile gloves instead of rubber ones, and avoid balloons. For condoms, there are latex-free ones made of polyurethane or polyisoprene that work well.
I didn’t know those existed.

They can slip or break a little more often, so use plenty of lubricant and know how to get emergency contraception. Would you like to think about a method that doesn’t rely on condoms, such as the pill, an implant, or a coil? Condoms would still protect against infections.
I’d like to think about it first.

Of course. I’ll give you information and you can book back or see the sexual health clinic. I’ll record the latex allergy clearly in your notes. Please tell every dentist, nurse or hospital before any procedure, including cervical screening, so they use latex-free gloves. A medical alert bracelet can help too.
I wouldn’t have thought of the smear test.
If you ever get swelling of your tongue or throat, difficulty breathing or swallowing, a hoarse voice, or feel faint after latex, call 999 straight away. For anything milder, come back and see me.
Okay.
Just to check I’ve explained it clearly, what will you do from now on?
Avoid latex, use nitrile gloves and latex-free condoms, tell dentists and nurses, wait for the allergy clinic, think about the other methods, and 999 if my throat swells.
That’s exactly it. I’ll send the referral today and see you when you’ve decided about contraception.

social.t: The reaction affects her sex life. Discuss openly and without embarrassment, and consider involving her partner in choosing latex-free condoms.
Latex is in gloves, balloons, some sports equipment and elastic. Practical avoidance at home matters as much as in healthcare.

legal.t: Under COSHH 2002, employers must assess and control exposure to latex, usually by using non-latex gloves. If she is exposed at work, occupational health can advise, and reasonable adjustments may apply.

professional.t: Record the allergy and the reaction type clearly so it appears on prescriptions and referrals (NICE CG183). Flag it on any referral for procedures.
Explain that anaphylaxis is uncommon but possible, without frightening or falsely reassuring her.

community.t: Sexual health clinics provide latex-free condoms and all contraceptive methods. Community pharmacists can supply latex-free condoms and emergency contraception.

redFlags: Tongue or throat swelling, breathing difficulty, hoarse voice, faintness or collapse after latex (999)
Widespread hives or reactions beyond the contact site
psychosocial: Impact on sex life and contraception
ice: Concern: it could get worse; unplanned pregnancy
Expectation: confirmation and a contraception solution

playbook.diagnosis: “This sounds like an immediate latex allergy, so far with reactions only where latex touches you.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your immune system has mistaken a protein in rubber for an invader, like a guard dog that barks at the postman. Each time latex touches you, the dog barks and the skin itches and swells. We can’t retrain the dog easily, so we keep the postman away.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought this was latex allergy, you were frightened by the lip tingling, and you need contraception you can rely on. You’re right about the allergy; let’s make you safe and sort contraception today.”
management.psychosocial: Discuss sex and contraception openly; include practical steps at home, at work and in healthcare.
sharedPlan: Refer to an allergy service for testing and risk assessment
Strict latex avoidance: nitrile gloves, no balloons
Polyurethane or polyisoprene condoms, lubricant, and emergency contraception advice (FSRH)
Offer other methods: pill, implant, injection or intrauterine methods
Record the allergy (NICE CG183); tell all healthcare and dental teams; medical alert bracelet
safetyNet: 999 for tongue or throat swelling, breathing difficulty or faintness
Review when she has chosen a contraceptive method or after the allergy clinic

pitfalls.intro: This station is lost by underestimating the risk, by vague avoidance advice, and by forgetting her contraception question. Each pattern below is common and fixable.

items.fail: Never asking about throat, breathing or faintness.
items.why: A systemic reaction changes urgency, referral and the auto-injector decision (NICE NG258).
items.fix: Ask directly about systemic features, especially around the lip episode.

items.fail: Calling it contact dermatitis without asking about timing.
items.why: Immediate reactions suggest type I allergy with anaphylaxis risk; delayed rashes suggest type IV.
items.fix: Ask how fast it starts and what it looks like.

items.why: Latex-fruit syndrome can cause reactions to banana, avocado, kiwi and chestnut.
items.fix: Ask about them and advise caution.

items.fail: Not recording the allergy or warning her about procedures.
items.why: Latex exposure in dental or hospital care can trigger severe reactions.
items.fix: Record it (NICE CG183) and tell her to inform every healthcare team, including for cervical screening.

items.why: It is half her agenda; unplanned pregnancy is a real risk.
items.fix: Offer latex-free condoms, emergency contraception advice and other methods.

items.why: She needs to recognise anaphylaxis and act.
items.fix: 999 for throat swelling, breathing difficulty or faintness; if an auto-injector is prescribed, carry two (MHRA 2023); teach-back.

timeMap.d: Hear both agendas: the reactions and contraception.
Timing and type of reaction, systemic features, exposures and work, atopy and operations, fruit reactions, current contraception.
Suspects latex allergy; frightened by lip tingling; wants reliable contraception.
Immediate latex allergy; honest anaphylaxis risk; allergy referral; auto-injector decision.
Avoidance, latex-free condoms and gloves, contraception options, recording, telling healthcare teams, 999 advice, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Advises an antihistamine and “try a different brand of condom”; never asks about throat or breathing symptoms; no allergy record or referral.
wordPics.pass: Recognises immediate latex allergy, screens for systemic features, advises latex-free condoms and gloves, refers to allergy and gives 999 advice.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: distinguishes type I from type IV; asks about work, risk groups and cross-reacting fruits; offers a full choice of contraception with emergency contraception advice; records the allergy and prepares her for procedures such as cervical screening; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Just try a different brand of condoms.”
avoid.instead: “Use latex-free condoms made of polyurethane or polyisoprene.”
avoid.why: Most standard condoms are latex; switching brand does not remove the allergen.

avoid.dont: “It’s only a skin reaction, nothing to worry about.”
avoid.instead: “It’s usually local, but because it can occasionally become severe, I want a specialist to assess you.”
avoid.why: Latex allergy can progress to anaphylaxis, especially with mucosal exposure.

avoid.dont: “Let’s test it by trying a glove here.”
avoid.instead: “The allergy clinic can confirm it safely with testing.”
avoid.why: Provocation outside a specialist setting risks a severe reaction.

Idea (latex allergy), concern (getting worse, unplanned pregnancy), expectation (confirmation and a contraception plan).
Referral for specific IgE or skin-prick testing; no in-practice challenge; records allergy status.
Type I latex allergy versus type IV contact dermatitis to rubber chemicals and irritant dermatitis.
Screens throat, breathing, faintness and generalised features; risk groups; latex-fruit cross-reactivity.
Probable immediate (IgE-mediated) latex allergy with local reactions only.
Strict avoidance with nitrile gloves and polyurethane or polyisoprene condoms; contraception options offered, with emergency contraception advice.
Tells healthcare and dental teams, including for cervical screening; COSHH and occupational health if exposed at work; medical alert.
999 for throat, breathing or faintness; allergy referral; review for contraception choice; teach-back.

social.t: The reaction affects her sex life. Discuss openly and without embarrassment, and consider involving her partner in choosing latex-free condoms.
Latex is in gloves, balloons, some sports equipment and elastic. Practical avoidance at home matters as much as in healthcare.

legal.t: Under COSHH 2002, employers must assess and control exposure to latex, usually by using non-latex gloves. If she is exposed at work, occupational health can advise, and reasonable adjustments may apply.

professional.t: Record the allergy and the reaction type clearly so it appears on prescriptions and referrals (NICE CG183). Flag it on any referral for procedures.
Explain that anaphylaxis is uncommon but possible, without frightening or falsely reassuring her.

community.t: Sexual health clinics provide latex-free condoms and all contraceptive methods. Community pharmacists can supply latex-free condoms and emergency contraception.

redFlags: Tongue or throat swelling, breathing difficulty, hoarse voice, faintness or collapse after latex (999)
Widespread hives or reactions beyond the contact site
psychosocial: Impact on sex life and contraception
ice: Concern: it could get worse; unplanned pregnancy
Expectation: confirmation and a contraception solution

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This sounds like an immediate latex allergy, so far with reactions only where latex touches you.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your immune system has mistaken a protein in rubber for an invader, like a guard dog that barks at the postman. Each time latex touches you, the dog barks and the skin itches and swells. We can’t retrain the dog easily, so we keep the postman away.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought this was latex allergy, you were frightened by the lip tingling, and you need contraception you can rely on. You’re right about the allergy; let’s make you safe and sort contraception today.”
management.psychosocial: Discuss sex and contraception openly; include practical steps at home, at work and in healthcare.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is lost by underestimating the risk, by vague avoidance advice, and by forgetting her contraception question. Each pattern below is common and fixable.

items.fail: Never asking about throat, breathing or faintness.
items.why: A systemic reaction changes urgency, referral and the auto-injector decision (NICE NG258).
items.fix: Ask directly about systemic features, especially around the lip episode.

items.fail: Calling it contact dermatitis without asking about timing.
items.why: Immediate reactions suggest type I allergy with anaphylaxis risk; delayed rashes suggest type IV.
items.fix: Ask how fast it starts and what it looks like.

items.why: Latex-fruit syndrome can cause reactions to banana, avocado, kiwi and chestnut.
items.fix: Ask about them and advise caution.

items.fail: Not recording the allergy or warning her about procedures.
items.why: Latex exposure in dental or hospital care can trigger severe reactions.
items.fix: Record it (NICE CG183) and tell her to inform every healthcare team, including for cervical screening.

items.why: It is half her agenda; unplanned pregnancy is a real risk.
items.fix: Offer latex-free condoms, emergency contraception advice and other methods.

items.why: She needs to recognise anaphylaxis and act.
items.fix: 999 for throat swelling, breathing difficulty or faintness; if an auto-injector is prescribed, carry two (MHRA 2023); teach-back.
